newsitem.title: UK: UK air cargo industry to set standards by end-'97.
newsitem.headline: UK air cargo industry to set standards by end-'97.

text.p: The UK air cargo industry is aiming to establish agreed performance standards by the end of this year, the UK Air Freight Forum said following its second meeting.
The proposal was unanimously adopted on Tuesday by the Forum which first met in November. It is made up of 20 major shippers, forwarders and airlines.

A sub-committee of nine Forum members - three from each sector - has been set up to "assess the key components of the entire logistical chain and identify ways in which common measurements can be put in place in order to effect an improvement in service delivery", the Forum statement said.
Shippers have agreed to take a critical look at how they can help forwarders and airlines make such improvements.
A key issue for shippers in the preparation of an air cargo industry "charter" or "code of conduct", is in giving details on cargo bookings to agents/forwarders.
Agents would then define this information and its accuracy in a checklist format before passing it to carriers to help achieve the best use of available air cargo capacity.
Other goals for shippers, said Forum chairman Des Vertannes of Air Canada, were agreed delivery times to agents, the definition of transit times and the clarification of expectations.

Forwarders' areas of responsibility should be providing assistance to carriers on space utilisation, making sure freight booked by shippers is made available and checking prompt collection times from shippers and delivery times to airlines.
Vertannes said airlines should make sure the best use if made of space and that cargo is "flown as booked", or otherwise good reasons are given for failure to meet this target.
Airlines should also determine accurate delivery cut-off times, truck waiting times prior to unloading and boarding on the aircraft, and unloading times.

The Forum also agreed airlines should provide accurate information to shippers and agents on cargo transit times. Asirlines should define import standards such as customs requirements and explain reasons for any possible delays.
Andrew Traill, shipping and air manager of the British Shippers' Council (BSC), said there will not be a "blacklist" of Forum members which fail to meet its standards.
But availability to the success of companies in meeting the targets would lead to "the market determining just who will be used" by the industry's various components.
The next meeting of the Forum is scheduled to be held at BIFA's headquarters in Feltham, Middlesex, near Heathrow, on May 15. - Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+ 5017
